items.why: The excerpt clearly contrasts the five spies who enter with the priest and soldiers who remain outside.
“First” makes this a useful sequence question because the five men take the items before the priest does.
The trees directly ask the thornbush to be their king, with little ambiguity.
The passage explicitly links prosperity to the land lacking nothing.
The stated reason is clear, while Israel’s lack of a king provides a plausible but distinct distractor.
The first sentence directly says Jotham lives there because he fears his brother Abimelek.
The addressees and the citizens who are to receive the message are clearly distinguished.
The question tests the Levite’s stated purpose rather than his eventual destination.
“Request just before the call for fire” is an artificial positional cue, and the conditional wish is not plainly a request.
“Does something” is too vague and forces readers to decode an underspecified pronoun rather than understand the event.
The reported news about the people entering the fields is clearly separated from what Abimelek later sees.
The mother’s wording names her son, but the later silversmith action creates a potentially confusing agent conflict.
The servant’s action and Abimelek’s death are stated directly and allow ordinary paraphrases.
The occupants die after the stronghold is set on fire, making the cause unmistakable.
The priestly term ends at the captivity, clearly distinguished from the idol’s use while Shiloh remained.
The wording explicitly connects the men’s shouting with the Danites turning, though overtaking is also nearby.
The fig tree’s rhetorical answer clearly presents giving up its sweet fruit as the cost of ruling.
The stated purpose of approaching the entrance is to set the tower on fire, not merely to attack it.
The command to go and take over the land is direct and distinguishes land from its inhabitants.
Micah explicitly gives the Levite’s becoming his priest as the reason for expecting God’s favor.
The intended location is recoverable, but “the residence the Danites visit” is needlessly cumbersome and artificial.
Jerub-Baal is the grammatical antecedent, but nearby Abimelek and the generic label “the man” make the reference harder than necessary.
Zebul is directly named as the angry governor who secretly sends the messengers.
The priest is identifiable from his reply, but the opening “said to him” lacks an explicit antecedent in the excerpt.
The curse is explicitly stated, but treating it as something happening after God’s punishment imposes a questionable sequence.
Zebul plainly calls them mountain shadows, though “what are they” has a mildly awkward pronoun reference.
Jotham explicitly asks them to listen so that God may listen to them, despite the slightly stiff question wording.
The olive tree clearly presents surrendering its honored oil as the reason not to rule.
Micah directly identifies his mother as the person who uttered the curse.
The passage clearly places the cursing during festival eating and drinking, after the grape work.
The excerpt gives two concrete reasons no rescue comes: distance from Sidon and lack of other relationships.
